title: Sea level rise weakens the restoration benefit of mussel–cordgrass facilitation in salt marshes
content:
Within a limited elevation range near the present marsh surface, ribbed mussels facilitate Spartina alterniflora biomass accumulation; however, this facilitative interaction is contingent on relative elevation and is likely to weaken as relative elevation declines under future sea level rise. Consequently, relative elevation provides a practical screening metric for marsh restoration efforts, helping to prioritize locations for incorporating ribbed mussels where benefits to cordgrass biomass are most likely and to avoid settings where expected benefits are low. This screening metric can inform marsh restoration project siting, monitoring and adaptive management under future sea level rise.


Abstract

Ribbed mussels are ecosystem engineers that can enhance the performance of Spartina alterniflora and contribute to shoreline protection, but it remains unclear how mussel facilitation of cordgrass growth and associated stability benefits vary across inundation gradients expected under accelerating sea level rise. Identifying where this facilitation strengthens or weakens along the elevation gradient is, therefore, essential for anticipating restoration outcomes and designing interventions that leverage biotic interactions under future inundation regimes. We conducted a field mesocosm experiment on the Louisiana coast using marsh organs planted with S. alterniflora. We exposed the plants to five elevation treatments (E = +5, 0, −5, −10 and −15 cm relative to the present marsh surface) to generate an inundation gradient spanning a low-inundation hindcast, present-day conditions and future relative elevation scenarios under sea level rise, and we crossed these elevations with four ribbed mussel (Geukensia granosissima) density treatments (N = 0, 254, 509 and 1018 individuals m−2). Our results showed that mussel–cordgrass facilitation was strongly dependent on relative elevation: increasing mussel density enhanced plant biomass accumulation only within a distinct ‘facilitation window’ where elevation keeps pace with sea level rise (+5 to 0 cm relative elevation). At relative elevations of −5 cm and lower, the positive mussel–cordgrass interaction weakened rapidly, forming a ‘decoupling zone’. Structural equation modelling further suggested that greater realized mussel biomass was associated with higher soil organic matter and below-ground biomass, whereas greater inundation frequency was associated with higher soil water content and lower soil organic matter and below-ground biomass. Synthesis and applications. Within a limited elevation range near the present marsh surface, ribbed mussels facilitate S. alterniflora biomass accumulation; however, this facilitative interaction is contingent on relative elevation and is likely to weaken as relative elevation declines under future sea level rise. Consequently, relative elevation provides a practical screening metric for marsh restoration efforts, helping to prioritize locations for incorporating ribbed mussels where benefits to cordgrass biomass are most likely and to avoid settings where expected benefits are low. This screening metric can inform marsh restoration project siting, monitoring and adaptive management under future sea level rise.
